title: Adjectives: agreement and position
summary: Adjectives change to match the noun and usually come after it. It also covers muy vs mucho and colours.
focus: Adjective agreement in gender and number, position, muy vs mucho
content:
## Adjectives agree with the noun

An adjective takes the **gender** and **number** of the noun it describes.

| ends in | masculine | feminine | plurals |
|---|---|---|---|
| **-o** | alto | alt**a** | altos / altas |
| **-e** | grande | grande | grandes |
| consonant | azul | azul | azul**es** |
| **-or** (people) | trabajador | trabajador**a** | trabajadores / trabajadoras |

- *un chico alto, una chica alta, unos chicos altos, unas chicas altas*
- *un coche grande, una casa grande, unos coches grandes*
- *un libro azul, una mesa azul, unos libros azules*

Nationalities ending in a consonant add **-a** in the feminine: *español → española*, *inglés → inglesa* (the accent disappears).

## Position: after the noun

Most adjectives come **after** the noun, the opposite of English. For example:

- *una ciudad bonita* (a pretty city)
- *el coche rojo* (the red car)

Quantity words come before: *muchos libros*, *pocas personas*, *otro día*. *Bueno* and *malo* can come before and shorten in the masculine singular: *un buen amigo*, *un mal día*.

## Muy vs mucho

- **muy** goes before an adjective or adverb and never changes: *muy alto, muy bien, muy rápido*.
- **mucho** before a noun agrees like an adjective: *mucho tiempo, mucha gente, muchos amigos, muchas cosas*.
- **mucho** after a verb never changes: *Trabajo mucho.* (I work a lot.)

So: *Es muy simpático y tiene muchos amigos.*

## Colours

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| rojo / roja: red | azul: blue | verde: green |
| amarillo / amarilla: yellow | negro / negra: black | blanco / blanca: white |
| gris: grey | marrón: brown | naranja: orange (same for both) |

*Rosa* and *naranja* are the same for masculine and feminine: *una camisa naranja*, *un coche naranja*. In the plural they usually stay the same too: *unas flores rosa* (*flores rosas* is also accepted).

vocabulary.example_meaning: There are a lot of people.

quiz.explanation: Casa is feminine singular, so the adjective ends in -a: pequeña.
Azul ends in a consonant: add -es for the plural, same for both genders.
Descriptive adjectives come after the noun.
Before a noun use mucho, agreeing with it: muchos amigos.
Before an adjective use muy, which never changes.
Nationalities ending in a consonant add -a in the feminine: española.

Naranja is the same for masculine and feminine: una camisa naranja, un coche naranja. Naranjo is the orange tree, and naranjas is plural. In the plural, camisas naranja and camisas naranjas are both accepted.
hints: Some colours are the same for masculine and feminine.

quiz.explanation: Adjectives in -e have one singular form for both genders: grande.

listening.note: Muy never changes; alta agrees with hermana.

listening.text: La casa es grande y bonita.
listening.meaning: The house is big and pretty.

listening.text: Las mesas verdes son muy baratas.
listening.meaning: The green tables are very cheap.

listening.text: Mi abuela tiene un perro pequeño y blanco.
listening.meaning: My grandmother has a small white dog.
listening.note: New word: el perro = the dog.

listening.text: Vivimos en una ciudad pequeña pero muy bonita.
listening.meaning: We live in a small but very pretty city.

listening.text: Mi hermano es alto, tiene los ojos verdes y un coche rojo muy grande.
listening.meaning: My brother is tall, has green eyes and a very big red car.

conversations.title: Describing a photo
conversations.scenario: Elena shows her friend Marcos a photo of her family.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Mira, esta es mi familia. Mi padre es el hombre alto.
lines.meaning: Look, this is my family. My dad is the tall man.

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: ¡Es muy alto! ¿Y la mujer de la camisa blanca?
lines.meaning: He's very tall! And the woman in the white shirt?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Es mi madre. Es pequeña pero muy fuerte.
lines.meaning: That's my mum. She's small but very strong.

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: ¿Quién es la chica del coche rojo?
lines.meaning: Who is the girl with the red car?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Mi hermana. Tiene muchos amigos y un coche nuevo.
lines.meaning: My sister. She has lots of friends and a new car.

lines.speaker: b
lines.meaning: What a pretty house! Is it big?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: No, es pequeña, pero el jardín es grande y verde.
lines.meaning: No, it's small, but the garden is big and green.

bites.title: Adjectives match the noun
bites.rule: An adjective takes its noun's gender and number: four tall girls are chicas altas, not altos.
bites.example: un chico alto, unas chicas altas
bites.example_meaning: a tall boy, some tall girls

bites.title: -e and consonants skip gender
bites.rule: Grande, verde, azul have the same form for men and women. They change only in the plural: grandes, azules.
bites.example: una casa grande, unos libros azules
bites.example_meaning: a big house, some blue books

bites.title: Noun first, then the adjective
bites.rule: Most adjectives come after the noun, the reverse of English: a red car is un coche rojo. Quantity words like muchos go before.

bites.title: Muy never changes, mucho does
bites.rule: Muy goes with adjectives and never changes; mucho goes with nouns and agrees: mucha gente, muchos amigos.
bites.example: Es muy simpático y tiene muchos amigos.
bites.example_meaning: He's very nice and has lots of friends.

sorts.title: Which noun does it fit?
sorts.why: The adjective's ending must match the noun's gender and number.

sorts.title: Muy or mucho?
sorts.why: Muy goes before adjectives and adverbs; mucho goes before nouns and agrees with them.

sorts.title: Does it change for a woman?
sorts.why: -o adjectives, -or words and nationalities add -a; -e, most consonant endings and naranja stay the same.

spots.why: Hermana is feminine, so the adjective is alta.
Plural noun, plural adjective: azul + es.
Before a noun you need mucho, agreeing: muchos amigos.
Nationalities add -a for a woman: española.
Casas is feminine plural, so pequeñas.
